Imaging of Cardiovascular Implantable Electronic Device Leads
With Photon-Counting Detector Computed Tomography
Simon Schalla, MD, PhD, Joachim E. Wildberger, MD, PhD, Mitch J.F.G. Ramaekers, MD, PhD,
Casper Mihl, MD, PhD, Michael C. McDermott, BSc, Lion Stammen, MSc, PhD,
Kevin Vernooy, MD, PhD, and Thomas G. Flohr, PhD
Objectives: Computed tomography (CT) imaging of cardiovascular implantable
electronic device (CIED) leads is currently hampered by large metal artifacts. Re-
cently, photon-counting detector CT (PCD-CT) has been clinically introduced,
offering high-resolution imaging with thin slice thicknesses and improved
contrast-to-noise ratios. Suspected complications of CIED such as perforation, in-
fection and venous obstruction could potentially be imaged with PCD-CT if
metal artifacts were effectively reduced through adapted scan protocols and iter-
ative metal artifact reduction algorithms (IMAR). The study evaluated the impact
of various scan and reconstruction parameters, including different IMAR settings,
on CIED lead visualization with PCD-CT in order to develop an optimized scan
and reconstruction protocol for imaging leads.
Materials and Methods: Five different CIED leads were evaluated in a nonbeating
heart phantom using a dual-source PCD-CTwith electrocardiography-gated spec-
tral standard resolution (collimation 144  0.4 mm) and nonspectral ultra-high res-
olution (UHR) mode (collimation 120  0.2 mm) spiral data acquisition. One scan
was performed for each lead and each acquisition mode. Images were reconstructed
with different slice thicknesses (0.2 mm, 0.4 mm, 0.6 mm), convolution kernels
(Bv40, Bv44, Bv48, and Bv56), virtual monoenergetic energy levels (60–140 keV
in steps of 10 keV), without and with different IMAR settings. The extent of metal
artifacts was objectively evaluated using 4 different parameters. Additionally, 3 ob-
servers subjectively assessed image quality using a 5-point scale.
Results: Metal artifacts increased with sharper kernels and higher keV levels in
virtual monoenergetic reconstructions. The artifacts were not dependent on slice
thickness. No significant differences in metal artifacts were observed between
UHR and standard-resolution scans when using similar reconstruction parame-
ters. IMAR effectively reduced artifacts across all kernels, slice thicknesses,
and keV levels, with the “neuro coils” setting showing the best performance. Sub-
jective analysis of image quality revealed that thinnest slices and sharpest kernels
(0.2 mm, Bv56) allowed for better delineation of fine structures, such as the shape
of helices, while reconstructions with thicker slices and softer kernels (0.6 mm,
Bv40) were preferred for visualizing general lead appearance and adjacent
anatomical structures.
Conclusions: Ultra-high and standard resolution PCD-CTwith IMAR enables good-
quality imaging of CIED leads, showing even small details without compromising the
visibility of nearby structures. A dedicated acquisition and reconstruction protocol
comprising an UHR scan with 2 reconstructions (0.2 mm/Bv56 and 0.6 mm/Bv40,
using IMAR) appears optimal for PCD-CT imaging of CIED leads.
Key Words: photon-counting CT, cardiovascular CT, CIED, pacemaker, ICD,
metal artifact, IMAR, CT reconstruction, ultra-high resolution

T
he role and optimal use of imaging modalities in patients with car-
diovascular implantable electronic device (CIED)-related compli-
cations has been evaluated, with each imaging technique offering spe-
cific advantages and disadvantages1: transthoracic echocardiography,
for example, is employed to rule out cardiac tamponade or lead-related
tricuspid valve regurgitation, transesophageal echocardiography to vi-
sualize specific parts of the leads to exclude the presence of vegeta-
tions. For pocket infections, positron emission tomography has shown
utility. Fluoroscopy and plain x-ray are routinely used during and after
implantation to assess lead position, offering high resolution and mini-
mal metal artifacts. However, spatial information as well as imaging of
soft tissue is limited and summation of image information into a single
plane can make it challenging to evaluate issues such as lead fractures.
Computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging of CIED
leads are currently hampered by large metal artifacts.2–4
Suspected complications of CIED, such as perforation, disloca-
tion, lead integrity, infection, and venous obstruction could be imaged
using CT if metal artifacts were efficiently reduced with, for example,
adaptation of scan parameters and iterative metal artifact reduction al-
gorithms (IMAR).5–7 Moreover, the assessment of coronary arteries
would be less hindered if metal artifacts from CIED leads could be
largely eliminated.
Recently, photon-counting detector CT (PCD-CT) was intro-
duced clinically.8 High-resolution imaging with thin slice thicknesses
and improved contrast to noise ratios became possible and was also ap-
plied to the field of cardiovascular imaging.9–11 Reduction of metal ar-
tifacts by cardiovascular PCD-CT could also be achieved.12 It may be
possible to visualize small structures, such as the helix at the tip of a
CIED lead, with better resolution and fewer metal artifacts using PCD-
CT, particularly if advances in metal artifact reduction are applied.8,13–17
Thus, the aim of the current study is to objectively and subjectively
assess the presence and extent of metal artifacts and the overall quality
of CIED lead visualization in electrocardiography (ECG)-triggered car-
diac CT scans using PCD-CT. The study evaluates the influence of differ-
ent convolution kernels, slice thicknesses, and energy levels of virtual
monoenergetic images (VMIs). These factors are examined both with
and without IMAR to define an optimized scan protocol for the best pos-
sible visualization of CIED leads and the adjacent anatomical structures.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
Phantom and CIED Leads
For the CT scans, a third-generation water-filled heart phantom
was employed, featuring a nonbeating 4-chamber heart with embedded
mitral and tricuspid valves, complete with chordae and papillary muscle
models.18 The phantom was manufactured using silicone printing tech-
nology, allowing for accurate lumen geometries (United Biologics Inc,
Santa Ana, CA).

Five different pacemaker and implantable cardioverter-defibrillator
(ICD) leads were investigated, representing the most common applications
in cardiac rhythm management (Table 1, Fig. 1). The leads were individu-
ally advanced through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle of the heart
phantom, and the tip of each lead was positioned in the apex of the right
ventricle (Fig. 2). The phantom was positioned within an oval-shaped ring
composed of fat-equivalent material (QRM, Möhrendorf, Germany) to
simulate the x-ray attenuation of a human thorax. The potential influ-
ence of osseous structures, such as ribs, was not taken into account.
CT Data Acquisition and Image Reconstruction
All scans were performed on a first-generation dual-source PCD-CT
(NAEOTOM Alpha, software version VA50; Siemens Healthineers AG,
Forchheim, Germany). ECG-gated spiral data were acquired, with an ar-
tificial ECG signal of 60 bpm, using 2 scan modes per CIED lead: a spec-
tral standard-resolution (collimation 144  0.4 mm) and a nonspectral
ultra-high resolution (UHR) mode (collimation 120  0.2 mm). The
ECG-gated modewas utilized to achieve the partial scan acquisition char-
acteristic of a cardiac scan. The gantry rotation time was 0.25 s, providing
a temporal resolution of 66 ms. Tube voltage was fixed at 140 kV. The
image quality (IQ) level was set to 62 with anatomical dose modulation
(Siemens CAREDose4D) turned on. UHR data were reconstructed as
polychromatic images with slice thicknesses of 0.2 mm, 0.4 mm, and
0.6 mm, using soft (Bv40), medium sharp (Bv44 and Bv48), and sharp
(Bv56) vascular kernels with quantum iterative reconstruction (QIR) at
strength 3, both without and with IMAR. Bv56 was the highest sharpness
level for which IMAR was available. For the 0.6-mm slice thickness, only
the Bv40 kernel was evaluated. This combination represents the typical
image sharpness in cardiac CT examinations with conventional energy-
integrating CT systems since sharper kernels are seldom used due to high
image noise and artifacts. To identify the most effective IMAR setting,
images with 0.2-mm slice thickness and Bv56 were first reconstructed
with all 8 available IMAR settings. The best-performing setting was then
used for all further reconstructions.
Standard-resolution data were reconstructed as VMIs from 60 to
140 keV in 10 keV increments, with 0.4-mm slice thickness and soft
(Bv40) and sharp (Bv56) vascular kernels with QIR at strength 3, both
without and with IMAR. The IMAR setting determined from the UHR
scans was used. In total, 2 scans and 45 reconstructions were conducted
for each CIED lead (Supplemental Digital Content Fig. A, http://links.
lww.com/RLI/B12).
All images were reconstructed with a matrix size of 512  512
and a field of view (FOV) of 150  150 mm2. Images were displayed
with the same window center [0 Hounsfield Units (HU)] and window
width (800 HU).
IMAGE EVALUATION
Objective Evaluation of Metal Artifacts Without and
With Metal Artifact Reduction
To objectively assess the severity of metal artifacts across various
scan and reconstruction parameters, both with and without IMAR, axial
images were selected at 3 different z-positions near the tip of each lead
(Fig. 2). These z-positions remained consistent for all reconstructions of
the respective lead.

For each lead at each z-position, one reconstruction was chosen
for each planned test (dependence on the IMAR setting, the convolution
kernel and slice thickness, and the VMI energy) to define the regions of
interest (ROI) for artifact analysis. Using an in-house Matlab program
(The MathWorks, Natick, MA), the following 3 steps were taken: a cir-
cular ROI was manually placed around the lead. Another ROI, referred
to as the reference ROI, was positioned in a distant homogeneous,
water-filled region minimally affected by artifacts. To exclude the lead
itself from the evaluation, all CT values above a threshold of 400 HU
were masked within the lead ROI (Fig. 3). This threshold was deter-
mined through testing to ensure that hyperdense metal artifacts were
minimally affected, allowing them to remain evaluable.
To ensure consistent analysis, the ROIs around the lead and lead
masks were copied into all further reconstructed images (with different
slice thicknesses, kernels, keV levels, or IMAR settings) of the lead at
the same z-position. The reference ROI was subjected to the same pro-
cedure when feasible. However, in cases where extensive metal artifacts
would compromise measurements in the reference ROI, minor adjust-
ments to its position or dimensions were implemented to mitigate inter-
ference. In addition, care was taken to ensure that the sizes of the ROIs
were as similar as possible across all z-positions and leads, minimizing
any potential influence of varying ROI sizes on the results.
For each ROI, the following 3 parameters were calculated: stan-
dard deviation of pixel values (in HU), mean pixel value (in HU) and
minimum pixel value (in HU). These measurements were used to derive
the following parameters characterizing the severity of metal artifacts,
partially based on the approach described by Risch et al.19:

This parameter quantifies the increase in image noise caused by
metal artifacts compared to the reference noise level. Without metal ar-
tifacts, AIX should be close to 0.
• The relative noise level σrelative is defined as the ratio of the standard
deviation of the pixel values in the ROI surrounding the lead σlead to

This parameter is particular useful when comparing the relative
severity of artifacts across reconstructions with different baseline refer-
ence noise levels σref, such as those resulting from various convolution
kernels and slice thicknesses. Without metal artifacts, σrelative should be
close to 1.
Our analysis focused on the following 4 key aspects:
1. Impact of IMAR type on metal artifact reduction. In this step, we
identified the most effective IMAR setting, which was used for all
further evaluations.
2. Effects of slice thickness and kernel on metal artifact severity, both
with and without IMAR
3. Influence of keV levels in VMIs on metal artifact severity, with and
without IMAR
4. Comparison of metal artifact severity between UHR and standard
resolution acquisition modes, both with and without IMAR
Additionally, the mean CT numbers of the CIED leads as a func-
tion of VMI energy (in keV) were measured. This analysis aimed to
draw conclusions about the metallic composition of the leads based
on the energy dependence of their CT numbers.
Subjective Analysis of IQ in Scan Reconstructions With
Metal Artifact Reduction
In addition to the objective evaluation of metal artifacts, we con-
ducted a subjective assessment of IQ for the UHR mode reconstructions
with IMAR, using various convolution kernels and slice thicknesses.
Three observers with different levels of experience [radiologist in
training (MR), 1 year of experience; radiologist (CM), more than 10 years
of experience; cardiologist (SS), more than 20 years of experience] scored
the images on a 5-point scale, assessing 2 main criteria: 1) visibility of fine
details (e.g., details of the helix at the tip), and 2) general IQ (e.g., extent of
metal artifacts, visibility of surrounding phantom-myocardium without ar-
tifact interference, appearance of leads). Given that all images with IMAR

Statistical Analysis
Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS, version 29.0
(IBM Corporate, Armonk, NY).
Objective IQ
All data were tested for normal distribution using the Shapiro-
Wilk test. Continuous variables are presented as mean and standard de-
viation or 95% confidence interval, as appropriate. The paired t test was
employed to assess significant differences in paired measurements (eg,
metal artifacts without and with IMAR, or between UHR and standard
resolution). A general linear model (ANOVA) was used to evaluate sig-
nificant differences in metal artifacts across various scan and recon-
struction parameters. Separate models were calculated for the depen-
dent variables Δ HU, HUmin, AIX
—–
, and σrelative. Kernel, slice thickness,
keV level, and IMAR setting were considered as independent variables.
To identify differences between various IMAR settings, kernels and
slice thicknesses, post-hoc analysis was performed. When the assump-
tion of homogeneity of variances was met, the Tukey test was applied.
In cases where this assumption was not met, the Games-Howell test
was used. In the case of multiple comparisons, P values were corrected
using the Bonferroni method. P values <0.05 were considered to
indicate statistically significant differences.
Subjective IQ
Interobserver agreements were assessed with the intraclass cor-
relation coefficient (ICC) by using a 2-way random method for absolute
agreement. The correlation coefficient ranges from 0 to 1, with 1 indi-
cating perfect agreement between different observers.21
RESULTS
Radiation Dose
The phantom scans resulted in a volume computed tomography
dose index (CTDIvol) of 4.9 ± 0.3 mGy for standard resolution and
9.3 ± 0.4 mGy for UHR scans.
Objective Evaluation of Metal Artifacts With and
Without Metal Artifact Reduction
Upon analysis, the metal artifacts produced by the 5 differ-
ent CIED leads showed similarity and similar dependencies (Sup-
plemental Digital Content Fig. B, http://links.lww.com/RLI/B13).
Given this consistency, we decided to average the artifact parame-
ters across all leads for subsequent investigations in order to en-
hance the clarity of data presentation and more effectively demon-
strate systematic dependencies.
Influence of IMAR Type on Metal Artifact Reduction
Figure 3 presents a typical example of metal artifacts without
IMAR and with 8 different IMAR settings (lead 2 is shown). Figure 4
illustrates the extent of metal artifacts with and without IMAR in cine-
matic volume rendering of images (lead 1). Metal artifacts were signif-
icantly reduced when IMAR was applied, compared to reconstructions
without IMAR. This observation held true for all 5 leads examined and
across all 3 evaluated artifact parameters (averaged AIX: P < 0.001;
HUmin: P < 0.001, Δ HU
—–: P < 0.043) (Fig. 5). Overall, the most effective
artifact reduction was achieved using IMAR setting 1 (“neuro coils”):
AIX decreased from 222.0 HU, 95% CI [203.0, 240.9] to 55.8 HU,
95% CI [45.4, 66.2] (Games-Howell P < 0.001), HUmin-from −727.4
HU, 95% CI [−875.1, −579.7] to −184.2 HU, 95% CI [−226.9,
−141.6] (P = 0.003), and Δ HU
—– from 32.6 HU, 95% CI [18.6, 46.6] to
6.8 HU, 95% CI [0.0, 13.7] (P = 0.047). Setting 1 was therefore used
for all further investigations.
Given the relatively high P value of Δ HU
—–, this parameter was ex-
cluded from further analysis. This decision was based on the observa-
tion that metal artifacts from CIED leads typically consist of both
hyperdense and hypodense components, as illustrated in Figure 3.
These opposing CT number deviations can cancel each other out, limit-
ing the parameter's usefulness in accurately characterizing the artifacts.

Artifact Severity
In the UHR scans reconstructed without IMAR, the reference re-
construction (kernel Bv40, slice thickness 0.6 mm) showed the least
severe metal artifacts on average. Without IMAR, the severity of metal

Influence of keV Level on Metal Artifact Severity
In the standard resolution scans reconstructed without IMAR
with kernel Bv56 at a slice thickness of 0.4 mm, metal artifacts showed
a significant dependence on the energy level of the VMIs (AIX: ANOVA
P = 0.005; HUmin: ANOVA P < 0.001) (Fig. 8, left). AIX increased from
192.0 HU, 95% CI [157.9, 226.2] at 60 keV to 227.9 HU, 95% CI [220.2,
235.7] at 140 keV, while HUmin decreased from −591.1 HU, 95% CI

DISCUSSION
This study evaluated the influence of different convolution ker-
nels, slice thicknesses, and energy levels of VMIs, both without and
with IMAR, on the presence and extent of metal artifacts as well as
the quality of visualization of CIED leads in ECG-triggered cardiac
PCD-CT scans in a nonbeating heart phantom. Metal artifacts, charac-
terized by both, the extent of hypodense artifacts (dark streaks) and im-
age noise caused by the artifacts, increased as kernel sharpness in-
creased. No significant dependence on slice thickness was observed,
which may be attributed to the leads being oriented almost perpendicu-
lar to the image plane. The relative increase in noise caused by metal ar-
tifacts compared to baseline image noise decreased significantly with
both increasing kernel sharpness and decreasing slice thickness. This
suggests that the baseline image noise increased more rapidly than the
metal artifact-induced noise when using sharper kernels and thinner
slices. Metal artifacts of CIED leads increased significantly with in-
creasing energy level (keV) of VMIs.
Previous studies with PCD-CT showed different results regarding
the correlation of metal artifact extent and keV level, depending on the
type of metallic implants: In the case of internal ankle fixations, smaller
artifacts were observed as keV levels increased. For total hip replacements,
an optimal energy level with minimal artifacts was achieved at 110 keV.

Dental implants showed artifacts that were relatively independent of keV
levels.23–25 We attribute our observed increase in metal artifacts at
higher keV levels to the metallic composition of the CIED leads: A
dual-energy analysis suggests that the leads contain metals with a high
atomic number. In fact, according to manufacturer's specifications, the
tip electrodes, ring electrodes, and coils are made of platinum (Z = 78)
alloys and platinum-clad tantalum (Z = 73). The CT number of high-Z
metals (measured in HU) and, consequently, the contrast between the
leads and their surrounding environment increases with higher keV
levels. This explains the increase in the extent of artifacts observed.
For the PCD-CT scanner evaluated, different IMAR settings
showed different potential for artifact reduction. Although none of the
settings had been specifically optimized for CIED leads, the best results
were achieved using the IMAR setting “neuro coils.” The application of
this setting significantly reduced metal artifacts from CIED leads across
all kernels, slice thicknesses, and keV levels. While the remaining arti-
fact level still showed significant dependence on kernel sharpness, it
was not affected by slice thickness. Unlike findings in other studies,
we observed no significant correlation between the remaining artifact
level and the VMI energy and there was no optimal energy level at
which metal artifacts were particularly minimized when using IMAR.
Both of these observations are likely due to the specific metallic compo-
sition of the CIED leads containing high Z-materials.24,26
With IMAR, the remaining artifact level showed, at most, a bor-
derline significant dependence on the acquisition mode (UHR or stan-
dard resolution) for identical kernel and slice thickness settings. The
better data sampling and reduced partial volume artifacts attributed to
the UHR mode did not lead to a significant reduction in metal artifacts
from CIED leads.
Application of IMAR using the “neuro coils” setting yielded di-
agnostically acceptable images for all leads, including both pacemaker
leads and the thicker, more metal-rich ICD leads. This high IQ was
maintained across various combinations of reconstruction kernels and
slice thicknesses, as determined by subjective IQ analysis. We therefore
anticipate that PCD-CT can be successfully employed to examine CIED
leads and potentially identify related complications. However, when
assessing CIED leads, reconstruction of 2 different image series may
be advantageous. A reconstruction using thicker slices (0.6 mm) and a
smoother kernel (Bv40) yielded the best subjective IQ when evaluating
regions adjacent to the lead. Notably, this combination resulted in min-
imal metal artifact interference in the surrounding myocardium. For
evaluating the lead itself, particularly its tip, thin slices (0.2 mm) and
sharp kernels (Bv56) were preferred, despite the significantly stronger
metal artifacts remaining after IMAR. This preference aligns with a pre-
vious study that recommended combining 0.2-mm slice thickness with
a sharper kernel to optimize visualization of fine details.27 In a study of
metal artifacts caused by left ventricular assist devices, the authors fa-
vored the combination of Bv56 and 3 mm slice thickness for minimiz-
ing metal artifacts, differing from our findings.26
There is a clinical need to image CIED leads to assess potential
postimplantation complications, including infection, tip dislocation, per-
foration, lead defects, or venous obstruction. Based on our findings, we
conclude that UHR-images (0.2 mm, Bv56) with IMAR are preferable
for evaluating lead fractures, while dislocations of the lead tip or perfo-
ration could be assessed by evaluating both image series (0.6 mm, Bv40
and 0.2 mm, Bv56) with IMAR. However, these recommendations re-
quire validation through further clinical studies.
Our study has some limitations. It utilized a static cardiac phan-
tom, which precluded assessment of cardiac motion's influence on
metal artifacts and their reduction through IMAR. Our study aimed to
investigate physics relationships, such as the dependence of metal arti-
facts on reconstruction sharpness, scan mode, and VMI energy. The in-
clusion of motion would introduce additional complexity, potentially
obscuring our conclusions and complicating the analysis of these spe-
cific physics relationships. A comprehensive evaluation of motion ef-
fects will be addressed in future studies. The leads in our phantom were
positioned almost perpendicular to the scan plane, and we did not exam-
ine other orientations. Consequently, we could not investigate the poten-
tial impact of slice thickness on metal artifacts for leads oriented differ-
ently. Key results, such as the determination of the most effective IMAR
setting or the keV dependence of artifacts, are expected to be indepen-
dent of lead orientation. A systematic investigation of various orienta-
tions (perpendicular to the scan plane, within the scan plane, and tilted
at 45°) will be the subject of a future study. While we assessed the visu-
alization of lead tips, we did not simulate lead perforations. Therefore,
we cannot currently evaluate how well perforations would be repre-
sented in CT images. We did not quantitatively measure metal artifacts
blurring in surrounding soft tissue. However, subjective assessment

In conclusion, the use of IMAR enables both ultra-high and stan-
dard resolution imaging of CIED leads with PCD-CT. This technique
achieves good IQ of the leads without compromising the visibility of
nearby structures. Based on our results, a dedicated acquisition and re-
construction protocol comprising an UHD scan with 2 reconstructions
(0.2 mm/Bv56 and 0.6 mm/Bv40, using IMAR) appears optimal for
PCD-CT imaging of CIED leads.
